title: Alluvial diagrams: follow one cohort through categorical stages
summary: Build ribbons from stable record identities, preserve the stage total, and distinguish an unobserved state from a measured exit.
body:
Build ribbons from stable record identities, preserve the stage total, and distinguish an unobserved state from a measured exit.

Start with the same population on every axis

An alluvial diagram follows records through a sequence of categorical observations. Each vertical axis is a stage or attribute; a ribbon groups records that share adjacent categories. The picture answers a different question from a general Sankey flow: which members of a fixed cohort changed category, and where did their recorded paths split? Establish the cohort before counting anything. If the first axis includes all accounts opened in April but the third includes every active account in June, the ribbon widths no longer describe transitions within one population. New entrants need a separate cohort or an explicit entrant category. Each record needs a stable identifier, a stage definition, and at most one category at a stage. A row count without identity cannot reveal whether the same seven accounts moved through the diagram or seven different accounts were sampled each time. Grain and denominators are the first validation gate.

Keep unobserved records in the ledger

A missing stage value is not automatically churn, failure, or inactivity. It may reflect a late data feed, an ineligible record, or a lost join. The worked contract keeps an explicit Not observed category so every axis and adjacent ribbon set still sums to the original cohort size. Analysts can then separate recorded churn from incomplete measurement. If the business meaning of absence is genuinely an exit, encode that as a distinct recorded event with a timestamp and an eligibility rule. Do not silently turn null into churn. Count each adjacent pair from the same record ledger; independently aggregated stage totals cannot reconstruct who crossed between categories. For a large diagram, group rare categories by a declared rule and keep an exact transition table. Cohort retention, missingness and linked filters show how the population can drift.

Order categories without inventing movement

Ribbon geometry depends on vertical category order. If each axis is reordered by its latest count, unchanged paths can cross even when the underlying records have not moved. Choose a domain order for each stage, version it, and hold it across comparable panels and exports. Keep a stable color meaning: color by the initial category when the question is origin, or by the final outcome when the question is destination. A gradient that changes meaning halfway through the diagram makes the path hard to decode. The ribbon width should represent count on a shared scale, while the hover text and adjacent table expose the exact count and denominator. Stage-specific percentages can be useful, but label their denominator; a ribbon of three out of four active trials is not the same quantity as three out of seven original accounts. Stacked bars are easier when only stage composition matters.

Design for inspection, not just spectacle

Crossing ribbons are expensive to trace by eye. Highlight a selected origin or destination, dim unrelated paths, and include a keyboard-accessible transition table with stage pair, source, destination and count. Do not make users identify a one-record path from a hairline ribbon. If there are many stages, provide a small-multiple view of adjacent pairs, then let a reader inspect one segment at a time. A stage with a newly introduced category should disclose the schema change; otherwise its ribbon can masquerade as behavioral movement. Preserve the filter state and cohort key in exported data. When identity cannot be linked across stages, the correct output is a sequence of separate category summaries, not an invented alluvial path. Keyboard access, export manifests and chord diagrams provide nearby design choices.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter

def build_account_alluvium(cohort_ids, stages, observations):
    if (not cohort_ids or len(set(cohort_ids)) != len(cohort_ids) or
            any(not isinstance(account_id, str) or not account_id.strip()
                for account_id in cohort_ids)):
        raise ValueError("cohort IDs must be unique nonempty strings")
    if (len(stages) < 2 or len(set(stages)) != len(stages) or
            any(not isinstance(stage, str) or not stage.strip() for stage in stages)):
        raise ValueError("at least two unique stages are required")
    cohort, stage_set = set(cohort_ids), set(stages)
    state_by_account_stage = {}
    for account_id, stage, state in observations:
        key = (account_id, stage)
        if (account_id not in cohort or stage not in stage_set or
                not isinstance(state, str) or not state.strip() or
                state == "Not observed" or key in state_by_account_stage):
            raise ValueError(f"invalid or duplicate observation: {key}")
        state_by_account_stage[key] = state

    def state_at(account_id, stage):
        return state_by_account_stage.get((account_id, stage), "Not observed")

    stage_counts = [Counter(state_at(account_id, stage) for account_id in cohort_ids)
                    for stage in stages]
    ribbons = [Counter((state_at(account_id, left), state_at(account_id, right))
                       for account_id in cohort_ids)
               for left, right in zip(stages, stages[1:])]
    assert all(sum(counts.values()) == len(cohort_ids) for counts in stage_counts)
    assert all(sum(counts.values()) == len(cohort_ids) for counts in ribbons)
    return stage_counts, ribbons

accounts = [f"AC-{number}" for number in range(41, 48)]
stages = ["intake", "trial", "renewal"]
observations = [
    ("AC-41", "intake", "direct"), ("AC-42", "intake", "direct"),
    ("AC-43", "intake", "referral"), ("AC-44", "intake", "referral"),
    ("AC-45", "intake", "partner"), ("AC-46", "intake", "partner"),
    ("AC-47", "intake", "direct"),
    ("AC-41", "trial", "active"), ("AC-42", "trial", "active"),
    ("AC-43", "trial", "inactive"), ("AC-44", "trial", "active"),
    ("AC-45", "trial", "active"), ("AC-46", "trial", "inactive"),
    ("AC-41", "renewal", "renewed"), ("AC-42", "renewal", "churned"),
    ("AC-43", "renewal", "churned"), ("AC-44", "renewal", "renewed"),
    ("AC-45", "renewal", "renewed"),
]
stage_counts, ribbons = build_account_alluvium(accounts, stages, observations)
assert stage_counts[2]["Not observed"] == 2
assert ribbons[1][("active", "renewed")] == 3
assert ribbons[1][("inactive", "Not observed")] == 1

Performance and operating cost

Let C be cohort size, S the number of stages, and R the number of supplied observations. Validating the observations and building the stage and adjacent-pair ledgers takes O(R + CS) time; storing the input lookup and aggregate counts takes O(R + CS) space in the worst case. In the worked seven-account cohort, three active trials become recorded renewals, one inactive trial has no renewal observation, and two accounts lack a renewal observation in total. Both adjacent ribbon sets still sum to seven. The code prepares counts; a renderer must apply a documented category order and a fixed width scale. Avoid drawing every record as its own ribbon when C is large: aggregate equal paths and retain the exact ledger for inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Building each stage from a different population and labeling the ribbons as cohort transitions.
  • Inferring a person's path from stage-level totals without stable record identity.
  • Treating a missing observation as a recorded exit or churn event.
  • Changing category order or color meaning between comparison panels.
  • Displaying percentages without naming whether the denominator is the original cohort or a stage subset.

Validation drill

Take a fixed cohort of 47 accounts observed at onboarding, first use and renewal. Verify one category per account per stage, preserve missing observations explicitly, reconcile every stage and ribbon set to 47, and publish a tabular list of the transitions that remain after rare categories are grouped.

title: Spectrograms: make time, frequency and color scales defensible
summary: Turn sampled signals into time–frequency cells with explicit window and hop lengths, a real amplitude reference, and an honest display floor.
body:
Turn sampled signals into time–frequency cells with explicit window and hop lengths, a real amplitude reference, and an honest display floor.

Every cell is a windowed estimate

A spectrogram shows how a sampled signal's frequency content changes over time. A row is a frequency bin, a column is a window position, and color encodes a defined measure such as amplitude or power. It is not a photograph of instantaneous frequency. Each column summarizes a finite stretch of samples; an abrupt event may influence several overlapping columns. Publish the sample rate, window length, hop length, window function, frequency units and color quantity. A signal sampled at 64 samples per second has a 32 hertz Nyquist frequency; frequencies above it cannot be uniquely represented without an anti-aliasing policy upstream. A 16-sample window lasts 0.25 seconds and places Fourier bins four hertz apart. Those are properties of the measurement contract, not choices to hide in rendering code. Time-series gaps and heatmap domains handle the adjacent display risks.

Choose window and hop for the question

A longer window separates nearby stable frequencies more finely, but it smears changes across more time. A shorter window localizes an event better while merging nearby frequencies. The hop controls how often the estimate is placed on the time axis; it does not create new information between samples. Overlap can make a display smoother, yet adjacent columns then share data and are not independent observations. A tapered window reduces the sharp edge introduced by slicing the signal, at the cost of spreading a bin-centered tone into neighboring bins. The worked example uses a Hann window, a 16-sample frame and an eight-sample hop. For a long recording, use a tested FFT implementation, cache only the visible range, and preserve the original sampling metadata. Level of detail matters before millions of cells reach a browser.

Label the decibel reference and floor

Decibels express a ratio, so a label that says dB without a reference is incomplete. The code computes an amplitude ratio against a reference amplitude of one and displays 20 times its base-ten logarithm. This is not calibrated sound-pressure level. A zero-amplitude bin would be negative infinity; the chosen minus-80-decibel floor keeps the display finite, and the legend must say that darker cells may be at or below that floor. Use the same color limits when comparing recordings. Rescaling each panel to its own maximum can make a quiet background resemble a loud event. Power or power spectral density requires a different normalization and should not be relabeled as amplitude. A log-frequency axis is another independent choice: it changes spacing on the vertical axis, not the contents of a Fourier bin. Axis rules and text alternatives prevent an attractive display from making an unsupported comparison.

Do not paint missing samples as silence

A telemetry dropout has no measured amplitude. Replacing it with zeros creates a vertical dark stripe and can inject a false transient at the gap boundary. Mark the affected windows as unavailable, or process only continuous spans and leave a visible break. Similarly, a microphone gain change or sensor recalibration can shift every color without changing the underlying event; annotate those changes and keep calibration metadata with the export. If a narrow bright line appears at one fixed frequency, check for machinery, power-line interference, sampling artifacts and window leakage before assigning a cause. For speech or music, the display can help locate intervals for listening, but color alone does not prove what produced a sound. Preserve the raw signal segment, transform parameters and render version in a chart export manifest.

Worked contract

from math import cos, hypot, isfinite, log10, pi, sin

def amplitude_spectrogram(samples, sample_rate, window_length, hop, floor_db=-80):
    values = list(samples)
    if (isinstance(sample_rate, bool) or not isinstance(sample_rate, (int, float)) or
            not isfinite(sample_rate) or sample_rate <= 0 or
            not isinstance(window_length, int) or isinstance(window_length, bool) or
            window_length < 4 or window_length % 2 or
            not isinstance(hop, int) or isinstance(hop, bool) or
            not 1 <= hop <= window_length or
            not isfinite(floor_db) or floor_db >= 0 or len(values) < window_length or
            any(isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float))
                or not isfinite(value) for value in values)):
        raise ValueError("invalid samples or transform settings")
    taper = [0.5 - 0.5 * cos(2 * pi * offset / (window_length - 1))
             for offset in range(window_length)]
    coherent_gain = sum(taper)
    frequencies_hz = [bin_index * sample_rate / window_length
                      for bin_index in range(window_length // 2 + 1)]
    amplitude_floor = 10 ** (floor_db / 20)
    columns = []
    for start in range(0, len(values) - window_length + 1, hop):
        frame = [values[start + offset] * taper[offset]
                 for offset in range(window_length)]
        levels_db = []
        for bin_index in range(len(frequencies_hz)):
            phase_step = 2 * pi * bin_index / window_length
            real = sum(value * cos(phase_step * offset)
                       for offset, value in enumerate(frame))
            imaginary = -sum(value * sin(phase_step * offset)
                             for offset, value in enumerate(frame))
            amplitude = hypot(real, imaginary) / coherent_gain
            if 0 < bin_index < window_length // 2:
                amplitude *= 2
            levels_db.append(20 * log10(max(amplitude, amplitude_floor)))
        center_seconds = (start + (window_length - 1) / 2) / sample_rate
        columns.append((center_seconds, levels_db))
    return frequencies_hz, columns

sample_rate = 64
signal = [sin(2 * pi * (8 if index < 32 else 16) * index / sample_rate)
          for index in range(64)]
frequencies, columns = amplitude_spectrogram(signal, sample_rate, 16, 8)
def strongest_frequency(levels):
    return frequencies[max(range(len(levels)), key=levels.__getitem__)]
assert strongest_frequency(columns[0][1]) == 8
assert strongest_frequency(columns[-1][1]) == 16
assert len(columns) == 7 and frequencies[-1] == 32

Performance and operating cost

With F windows of W samples, this transparent direct Fourier transform costs O(FW²) time and O(FW) space for a complete output matrix. Production FFT implementations reduce transform work to roughly O(FW log W), while a streamed renderer can bound memory to the visible columns. The sample uses 64 samples per second, 16 samples per window and an eight-sample hop: seven columns, four-hertz bin spacing, a 32-hertz Nyquist limit and one-half overlap. Its first complete window is strongest at eight hertz, while the final complete window is strongest at sixteen hertz. The intermediate windows mix the two segments. The decibel values are relative amplitudes, with a minus-80-decibel display floor; they are not a calibrated loudness measurement.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling adjacent overlapping windows independent measurements.
  • Using a larger hop and claiming it improves the underlying time resolution.
  • Labeling relative amplitude decibels as calibrated sound-pressure levels.
  • Choosing a new color minimum and maximum for every panel that must be compared.
  • Replacing missing samples with zeros and reading the resulting stripe as silence.

Validation drill

Analyze a 47-second machine recording with a declared sample rate. Freeze window, hop, taper, reference and color bounds before comparing it with another run. Mark any sample gaps, inspect whether a detected stripe survives a different window length, and export the transform settings beside the cells.

title: Raincloud plots: show the estimate, summary and records together
summary: Combine a density silhouette, quartile summary and stable raw points without hiding unequal group sizes or bandwidth choices.
body:
Combine a density silhouette, quartile summary and stable raw points without hiding unequal group sizes or bandwidth choices.

Three layers answer three questions

A raincloud plot places a distribution estimate, a compact summary and individual observations beside one another for each group. The density shape helps locate concentrations, the quartiles orient a comparison, and raw points reveal outliers, ties and sample size. None of the layers should be allowed to contradict another through a hidden filter. Use the same eligible records for all three, then display the count near each group. For service latency, a broad-looking density may come from seven observations while a narrow-looking one may come from hundreds; if both are normalized to area one, shape width is not a record count. Keep a shared value axis and state whether the density is normalized within each group or scaled to count. A simple box or violin plot may be clearer when there are many groups. Beeswarm points are a better raw layer when exact overlaps matter.

Freeze smoothing and value bounds

The cloud is a model of a distribution, not a trace of every observation. A Gaussian kernel density estimate spreads each record over nearby values according to a bandwidth. Too little smoothing turns each value into its own bump; too much erases shoulders or separated clusters. For a comparison, use one declared bandwidth in the measured unit and one common grid. If groups are measured on different units, convert them before plotting or keep separate panels. The example below uses a fixed bandwidth of two minutes and a grid spanning every observed value plus three bandwidths on each side. That avoids trimming the visible tails differently by group. It also keeps the half-violin widths as within-group density, so their maximum heights should not be read as a sample-size comparison. Histogram density offers another check on smoothing.

Keep raw points stable and quartile policy explicit

A little horizontal jitter separates identical or nearly identical values, but jitter must not alter the measured axis. The code derives a stable display offset from each record identifier, so refreshing a dashboard does not make the same observation jump to a random place. It does not guarantee that all points are collision-free; densely repeated values may still need a beeswarm algorithm or a count label. The quartiles use one named calculation policy, and the same policy must be used for every group and exported summary. A whisker rule should also be named if whiskers are drawn. The worked ledger omits them rather than letting a plotting library silently choose. When records are paired across groups, a raincloud can conceal that relationship; a connected paired display is more appropriate for the primary comparison. Paired change charts preserve identity.

Choose a view that survives small screens

A cloud, box and points can become three cramped marks on a phone. Keep the value axis labeled, leave room for group names, and offer a table with count, median, quartiles and every raw value when feasible. A screen reader should not announce a hundred decorative cloud coordinates; it needs the group summary and a path to the underlying records. If a small group contains only a handful of observations, the smoothed cloud can imply more certainty than the data warrant. Show the points and summary first, and either omit the density or label it as exploratory. If a record disappears under a filter, recompute all three layers from the same filtered population. Small-sample display, accessible alternatives and shared facets help keep the comparison honest.

Worked contract

from hashlib import blake2s
from math import exp, isfinite, pi, sqrt
from statistics import median, quantiles

def prepare_latency_raincloud(groups, bandwidth_minutes, grid_size=41):
    if (not groups or not isinstance(bandwidth_minutes, (int, float)) or
            isinstance(bandwidth_minutes, bool) or not isfinite(bandwidth_minutes) or
            bandwidth_minutes <= 0 or not isinstance(grid_size, int) or
            isinstance(grid_size, bool) or grid_size < 3):
        raise ValueError("invalid groups, bandwidth or grid size")
    all_minutes = []
    for group_name, records in groups.items():
        if not isinstance(group_name, str) or not group_name.strip() or len(records) < 4:
            raise ValueError("each named group needs at least four records")
        record_ids = [record_id for record_id, _ in records]
        if (len(set(record_ids)) != len(record_ids) or
                any(not isinstance(record_id, str) or not record_id.strip()
                    for record_id in record_ids)):
            raise ValueError("record IDs must be unique within each group")
        for _, minutes in records:
            if (not isinstance(minutes, (int, float)) or isinstance(minutes, bool) or
                    not isfinite(minutes) or minutes < 0):
                raise ValueError("latencies must be finite nonnegative minutes")
            all_minutes.append(minutes)
    lower = min(all_minutes) - 3 * bandwidth_minutes
    upper = max(all_minutes) + 3 * bandwidth_minutes
    grid = [lower + (upper - lower) * index / (grid_size - 1)
            for index in range(grid_size)]
    prepared = {}
    for group_name, records in groups.items():
        minutes = sorted(value for _, value in records)
        first_quartile, _, third_quartile = quantiles(minutes, n=4, method="inclusive")
        density = [sum(exp(-0.5 * ((position - value) / bandwidth_minutes) ** 2)
                       for value in minutes) /
                   (len(minutes) * bandwidth_minutes * sqrt(2 * pi))
                   for position in grid]
        points = []
        for record_id, value in records:
            digest = blake2s(record_id.encode(), digest_size=4).digest()
            display_offset = (int.from_bytes(digest, "big") / 2**32 - 0.5) * 0.2
            points.append((record_id, value, display_offset))
        prepared[group_name] = {"count": len(minutes), "median": median(minutes),
                                "quartiles": (first_quartile, third_quartile),
                                "density": density, "points": points}
    return grid, prepared

queue_minutes = {
    "north": [("N-41", 12), ("N-42", 13), ("N-43", 14), ("N-44", 14),
              ("N-45", 15), ("N-46", 16), ("N-47", 27)],
    "south": [("S-51", 11), ("S-52", 12), ("S-53", 12), ("S-54", 13),
              ("S-55", 18), ("S-56", 19), ("S-57", 20), ("S-58", 21)],
}
grid, clouds = prepare_latency_raincloud(queue_minutes, bandwidth_minutes=2)
assert len(grid) == 41 and clouds["north"]["median"] == 14
assert clouds["south"]["median"] == 15.5
assert len(clouds["north"]["points"]) == 7

Performance and operating cost

Let N be the total observations across G groups and M the number of shared grid positions. Sorting within groups costs at most O(N log N); direct Gaussian density evaluation costs O(MN). Storage is O(N + GM) for raw points and density arrays. The two queue groups contain seven and eight recorded durations. North's median is 14 minutes; south's is 15.5. Both clouds use the same two-minute bandwidth and common value grid. Their density curves are normalized within group, so a taller peak does not mean more records. The stable identifier-derived offset affects only a point's cross-axis display position; the latency value and quartile calculation remain unchanged. For very large N, choose a tested KDE implementation or a binned approximation, and state the approximation in the export.

Common Mistakes

  • Letting each group or refresh pick its own bandwidth and then comparing the apparent number of modes.
  • Interpreting equal-area density height as a sample count.
  • Moving raw points along the measured value axis while calling it harmless jitter.
  • Computing the cloud, quartiles and raw points from different filtered subsets.
  • Hiding small group sizes behind a smooth cloud or omitting the quartile calculation policy.

Validation drill

Compare two service queues with 47 and 83 eligible requests. Use one value domain and one predeclared bandwidth, keep every raw duration tied to a stable request ID, label both sample sizes, and check whether an apparent second peak remains after viewing the points and a binned histogram.

title: Data Visualization Tutorial
summary: Design auditable charts from explicit populations, stable scales, visible uncertainty and accessible representations.
body:
Design auditable charts from explicit populations, stable scales, visible uncertainty and accessible representations.

Learning path

  • Chart design starts with a question, unit and visual encoding
  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
  • Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
  • Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
  • Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone
  • Dashboard filters and provenance: make every view reproducible
  • Project: build an auditable receipt-review dashboard

Connected foundations

Use the earlier data and model boundaries as prerequisites.

  • Data Science for Beginners
  • Applied Statistics Tutorial

Practice

  • Data Visualization: Projects

Continue into another subject: Geospatial Analytics Tutorial.

For the full track and its related lessons, open Data visualization.

Time, density, facets and matrices

  • Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
  • Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
  • Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
  • Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit

Maps, interaction, scale and exports

  • Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
  • Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
  • Large chart series: reduce marks without erasing spikes
  • Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together

Composition, scales and paired comparisons

  • Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
  • Logarithmic axes: disclose zero handling and the linear threshold
  • Paired-change charts: match entities before drawing a slope
  • Empirical CDFs: read thresholds and tails without choosing bins

Flow, hierarchy, networks and events

  • Sankey diagrams: reconcile flows before sizing links
  • Treemaps: validate hierarchy and leaf totals before assigning area
  • Network graphs: define nodes and edges before trusting the layout
  • Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality

Distribution and association

  • Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
  • Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color

Forecasts and conversion

  • Forecast fan charts: label interval meaning and forecast horizon
  • Funnel charts: hold the cohort still before calculating conversion

Dense points and signed gaps

  • Hexbin density: count overlapping points without hiding exposure
  • Diverging bars: put signed differences on one shared zero

Bridges, targets and dual axes

  • Waterfall charts: reconcile every step to the closing total
  • Bullet charts: show a measure, target and performance bands honestly
  • Dual-axis charts: test whether two series really need one plot

Individual marks and complete days

  • Beeswarm plots: show individual values without inventing spread
  • Calendar heatmaps: distinguish an empty day from an absent day

Profiles, ranks and process limits

  • Parallel coordinates: make every axis conversion inspectable
  • Bump charts: show rank movement without losing ties or entrants
  • P charts: account for varying denominators before flagging a rate

Cumulative totals, uncertainty and quantiles

  • Pareto charts: reconcile the cumulative line to the categories
  • Asymmetric error bars: tell readers what each endpoint means
  • Q–Q plots: compare distribution shape beyond one summary number

Mapped symbols and task timelines

  • Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
  • Gantt timelines: make task dates and dependencies auditable

Distributions, fits and mapped routes

  • Ridgeline plots: compare distributions without hiding their size
  • Regression overlays: separate fitted trend from individual spread
  • Map boundaries: handle antimeridian crossings before drawing routes

Event alignment and chart interaction

  • Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
  • Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer

Effect estimates and multivariable grids

  • Forest plots: align estimates, intervals and the no-effect value
  • Scatterplot matrices: disclose which rows support each pair

Compact and moving time series

  • Streamgraphs: preserve totals behind a moving baseline
  • Horizon charts: trade vertical space for a harder value lookup
  • Animated charts: do not let motion invent data

Event and category evidence

  • Survival curves: show who remains at risk after each event
  • Mosaic plots: make cell area match the underlying count

Compositions and process signals

  • Ternary plots: preserve the total behind a three-part composition
  • CUSUM charts: accumulate small departures from a stable target

Flow and geographic comparisons

  • Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
  • Bivariate choropleths: map two rates with a readable joint legend

Hierarchy and probability evidence

  • Dendrograms: read merge height without overreading leaf order
  • Probability calibration plots: compare predicted risk with observed frequency

Model decisions and measurement agreement

  • Precision–recall curves: preserve threshold ties and class prevalence
  • Bland–Altman plots: assess paired measurement agreement

Set intersections and spatial surfaces

  • UpSet plots: count exact intersections without double counting
  • Contour plots: respect measured grids and interpolation boundaries

Classification decisions and errors

  • ROC curves: read attainable thresholds and false-positive rates
  • Confusion matrices: fix class order, denominators and abstentions

Monitoring slow process shifts

  • EWMA control charts: detect slow shifts against a frozen baseline

Ranked outreach and regression checks

  • Cumulative gains and lift: rank contacts without hiding score ties
  • Regression residual plots: locate bias, spread and missing segments

Population structure and comparison

  • Population pyramids: compare age bands without losing the denominator

Inequality and ranked shares

  • Lorenz curves: audit ranked shares before quoting a Gini value

Process variation and scenario sensitivity

  • Individuals and moving-range charts: monitor level and local variation
  • Tornado charts: keep scenario ranges attached to their assumptions

Distribution area and cohort maturity

  • Unequal-bin histograms: make rectangle area carry frequency
  • Cohort retention heatmaps: keep immature cells blank

Serial dependence and seasonal evidence

  • Autocorrelation plots: align equal-spaced periods before reading lag peaks

Observed spread and defect-rate monitoring

  • Historical percentile ribbons: show the spread of observations over time
  • U charts: monitor defect counts when inspection exposure changes

Seasonal pattern diagnostics

Where to begin

title: Sankey diagrams: reconcile flows before sizing links
summary: Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.
body:
Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.

A link represents a transfer

A Sankey diagram uses link width to encode quantity moving between stages. The visual claim is stronger than a list of counts: a unit leaving one stage must either enter a named next stage, exit the process, or remain unobserved under a declared cutoff. If 81 claims enter triage and 47 reach review, the other 34 need a visible destination, not an unexplained gap. Unit-of-analysis rules prevent one claim with multiple events from becoming several flows.

Give nodes stage-specific identities

The same label at two stages does not necessarily describe the same state. Use stable stage and state IDs, deduplicate by entity and transition, and decide how repeated or backward transitions are handled. A diagram that assumes a directed acyclic process can fail when work returns to triage. In that case, either aggregate one chosen journey window or use another graph view that represents loops. Network diagrams can show cycles, though they answer a different question.

Check conservation at intermediate stages

For a closed interval, incoming and outgoing measured quantities at a transit state should balance after explicit additions, losses and stock change. If 47 enter review and 42 leave, five may still be in progress; add a pending exit or annotate the stock. For a live interval, arrivals and departures can differ because the cohort has not matured. Attach extraction time and observation horizon to the flow, and never compare incoming of one cohort to outgoing of another. Provisional periods need separate handling.

Make ordering and scale inspectable

Link crossing is partly a layout choice. Reordering nodes can reduce crossings without changing the data, so visual proximity must not be treated as a causal relation. Show quantities, units and denominators in text or a companion table. Fixed link colors can track origin across stages, but blending may obscure a small branch; direct labels or hover summaries help. Accessible alternatives should list source, target and value. Large graphs may be better as a transition table.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def reconcile_flow(
    links: list[tuple[str, str, int]], transit_nodes: set[str]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, quantity in links:
        if not source or not target or quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("invalid flow link")
        outgoing[source] += quantity
        incoming[target] += quantity
    balances = {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in transit_nodes}
    if any(entered != left for entered, left in balances.values()):
        raise ValueError(f"unreconciled transit node: {balances}")
    return balances

journey = [("intake", "review", 47),
           ("intake", "unobserved-exit", 34),
           ("review", "closed", 42),
           ("review", "pending", 5)]
assert reconcile_flow(journey, {"review"}) == {"review": (47, 47)}
assert sum(value for source, _, value in journey if source == "intake") == 81

Performance and operating cost

For E links and T transit nodes, accumulation and reconciliation take O(E + T) expected time and O(V) space for V encountered nodes. Layout can be substantially more expensive and depends on the rendering algorithm; do not mix that cost with the inexpensive accounting check. A real workflow also checks duplicate entity transitions and whether stock change belongs in the diagram. The example treats all links as counts in one cohort and one period.

Common Mistakes

  • Hiding exits to make the main path look complete.
  • Counting multiple events from one entity as separate stage transfers.
  • Balancing one period's arrivals against another period's departures.
  • Assuming node position or link crossing has business meaning.

Validation drill

Model 81 claims through intake, review and closure. Add a pending branch and an unobserved exit; fail the reconciliation when either is removed, then render a transition table beside the flow.

title: Cohort retention heatmaps: keep immature cells blank
summary: Fix first-entry membership, define the return event and reserve zero for a mature period with no returning members.
body:
Fix first-entry membership, define the return event and reserve zero for a mature period with no returning members.

Anchor each member once

A cohort retention heatmap groups entities by a first qualifying period, then shows the share that performs a specified return action at each elapsed age. Rows are entry cohorts; columns are ages, not calendar dates. The entity might be a user, account or device, and those IDs are not interchangeable. Deduplicate signup records, resolve identity before grouping and keep each member in the original cohort. If a person returns after an inactive week, they still belong to their first cohort. Choose the return event precisely: opening the app, completing a project and making a payment yield different retention curves. Grain and denominator rules prevent an event count from masquerading as a user count. Funnels answer a related but different progression question.

Hold the original denominator fixed

In return-in-period retention, the numerator at age three is the number of original cohort members active in that period; the denominator is the size of that original eligible cohort. Do not divide by last week's active members unless the chart explicitly measures conditional continuation. Several return events by one member in the same period count once. An age-zero cell is one only if it represents enrollment by definition; it is not automatically one when age zero requires a distinct return action. State whether the chart means activity in that exact period, any activity up to that period, or continuous activity in every period. Those definitions can reverse the visual impression. Linked filters must recalculate cohort membership and denominator together rather than filtering only the numerator.

Separate zero from not yet observed

A young cohort has not reached later ages. Its future cells are undefined, not zero percent. A mature cohort with no returning member has a genuine zero. The current partial week is another state: until it closes, all cohorts' cells for that calendar week are provisional, because an apparent decline can simply be missing future activity. Keep a last-complete-period watermark, emit blank cells beyond it and label the watermark on the display. The triangular blank region should use a distinct missing pattern or text, not the low-retention color. Older data can still be incomplete because event ingestion is delayed; an as-of timestamp and an ingestion-lag audit should accompany published comparisons. Heatmap missingness and period completeness provide the display contract.

Compare equal ages and adequate support

Reading down one age column compares groups at the same lifecycle point; reading diagonally compares the same calendar period across groups of different ages. The latter can reveal a platform outage, but it is not a direct retention comparison. Show cohort sizes because 50 percent may represent one of two members or 5,000 of 10,000. Keep one zero-to-one color range across all rows and do not stretch each row independently. For small cohorts, add counts or uncertainty intervals and avoid strong claims from a bright cell. Segment-specific charts need an eligibility rule frozen at entry; defining a segment using future behavior leaks outcomes into cohort assignment. Small-sample display and calendar completeness help audit this comparison.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def retention_ledger(enrollments: list[tuple[str, int]],
                     return_events: list[tuple[str, int]],
                     last_complete_period: int, max_age: int):
    if max_age < 0 or not isinstance(last_complete_period, int):
        raise ValueError("age and complete-period watermark must be valid")
    entry = {}
    cohorts = defaultdict(set)
    for member_id, period in enrollments:
        if not member_id or member_id in entry or period > last_complete_period:
            raise ValueError("members need one completed entry period")
        entry[member_id] = period
        cohorts[period].add(member_id)
    if not entry:
        raise ValueError("at least one enrolled member is required")
    returned = defaultdict(set)
    for member_id, period in return_events:
        if (member_id not in entry or period < entry[member_id] or
                period > last_complete_period):
            raise ValueError("return event falls outside the observed member history")
        returned[(entry[member_id], period - entry[member_id])].add(member_id)
    rows = []
    for cohort_period in sorted(cohorts):
        size = len(cohorts[cohort_period])
        cells = [1.0]
        for age in range(1, max_age + 1):
            cells.append(None if cohort_period + age > last_complete_period
                         else len(returned[(cohort_period, age)]) / size)
        rows.append((cohort_period, size, cells))
    return rows

members = [("member-47", 47), ("member-59", 47), ("member-83", 47),
           ("member-97", 48), ("member-131", 48), ("member-149", 49)]
returns = [("member-47", 48), ("member-47", 48), ("member-83", 48),
           ("member-47", 49), ("member-97", 49)]
heatmap = retention_ledger(members, returns, last_complete_period=49, max_age=2)
assert heatmap[0] == (47, 3, [1.0, 2 / 3, 1 / 3])
assert heatmap[1] == (48, 2, [1.0, 1 / 2, None])
assert heatmap[2] == (49, 1, [1.0, None, None])

Performance and operating cost

For E enrollments, A return records, C cohorts and H requested ages, membership construction and event deduplication take O(E + A) expected time; sorting cohort keys takes O(C log C), and cell construction takes O(C·H). The entry and activity sets use O(E + A) space in the worst case, with O(C·H) output cells. Duplicate age-one activity from member-47 still counts once, while the newest cohort's future cells are None rather than zero. Period integers stand for consecutive, fully closed reporting periods; use a calendar-aware key upstream when weeks or months cross time-zone or fiscal boundaries.

Common Mistakes

  • Reassigning a returning member to a new entry cohort.
  • Dividing by the previous period's active members while labeling the result cohort retention.
  • Painting future or partial-period cells as zero percent.
  • Counting duplicate return events as multiple retained users.

Validation drill

Build weekly retention for 47 synthetic signup cohorts with a fixed last-complete-week watermark. Reconcile unique entry IDs, duplicate activity events and cohort sizes; publish age-one and age-four counts as well as rates, and leave all immature cells blank.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Validation drill

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.

title: Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
summary: Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.
body:
Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.

Fix the unit and direction first

A chord diagram curls a square flow matrix around a circle. One row identifies the source; one column identifies the destination. A matrix entry can represent parcels moved between depots, but it cannot mix parcel count with shipment value. Decide whether the story is directed before any ribbons are drawn: a transfer from North to East is not the same record as East to North. If the values describe mutual relationships rather than movements, use an undirected contract and explain how two mirrored cells are consolidated. Network graphs emphasize topology; chords emphasize the volume between a manageable set of named groups. Their apparent symmetry can mislead readers when source and destination have different meanings, so label the ends or use a visible directional cue.

Reconcile sectors and ribbons

For a directed matrix, the outbound total of a group is its row sum and inbound total is its column sum. Decide whether each sector encodes outbound alone or inbound plus outbound; otherwise a sector width may appear to contradict its label. The worked contract below reports both. A transfer from a group to itself belongs on the diagonal and must be kept or explicitly excluded. Draw a self-loop distinctly because it can consume a large share of an arc without crossing the center. A ribbon should have an auditable value in an accompanying table. Sankey diagrams are often clearer when a process has ordered stages and conservation across them must be inspected.

Keep categories and filters stable

Arc order changes which ribbons overlap and can make the same data look dense or sparse. Set one documented category order across periods and filtered views. If an unseen group is grouped into Other, publish which group IDs it contains and keep its membership fixed when comparing periods. An interaction should reveal source, destination, amount, unit, time window and whether the value is a self-loop. It should also disclose the current filter cohort. Linked filter state is part of the reading contract: a selected destination must not silently redefine the total behind each sector. Export the full matrix rather than only the visible top ribbons.

Use density as a stopping rule

With 47 groups, there can be 2,209 directed cells before any filtering. Even a complete and accurate chord can become an unreadable knot. Start with a ranked table, a small set of stable groups or a matrix heatmap when precise cell comparisons matter. Heatmaps preserve a fixed row-column grid and make absent flows easier to spot. If the chord is retained, annotate whether zeros mean no observed movement or unavailable data, and provide text alternatives for keyboard and screen-reader access. Test the display at narrow widths; hiding labels does not remove the underlying ambiguity.

Worked contract

def directed_flow_ledger(groups: list[str],
                         flows: dict[tuple[str, str], int]):
    if not groups or len(groups) != len(set(groups)) or any(not name for name in groups):
        raise ValueError("group names must be unique and nonempty")
    known = set(groups)
    if any(source not in known or target not in known or
           type(amount) is not int or amount < 0
           for (source, target), amount in flows.items()):
        raise ValueError("flow endpoints and amounts must be valid")
    matrix = [[flows.get((source, target), 0) for target in groups]
              for source in groups]
    outbound = {source: sum(matrix[index])
                for index, source in enumerate(groups)}
    inbound = {target: sum(matrix[index][column]
                           for index in range(len(groups)))
               for column, target in enumerate(groups)}
    assert sum(outbound.values()) == sum(inbound.values())
    return matrix, outbound, inbound

depots = ["North", "East", "West"]
transfers = {("North", "East"): 47, ("East", "North"): 13,
             ("North", "North"): 5, ("West", "East"): 29}
matrix, outbound, inbound = directed_flow_ledger(depots, transfers)
assert matrix[0] == [5, 47, 0]
assert outbound["North"] == 52
assert inbound["East"] == 76
assert sum(outbound.values()) == 94

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, matrix construction takes O(G²) time and O(G²) space even when most flows are zero. The sparse input map is better for storage and for very large networks; the dense matrix is useful only when the chosen renderer requires it. The ledger counts each directed transfer once, including a self-loop, and proves that aggregate outbound equals aggregate inbound. It does not turn the chart into a conservation model across time: inventory changes and external entries still require their own rows.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding both directions into one ribbon while calling the result directed.
  • Dropping self-loops because they do not cross the circle.
  • Changing arc order or the membership of Other between comparison panels.
  • Treating an unavailable matrix cell as an observed zero.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Large chart series: reduce marks without erasing spikes
summary: Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.
body:
Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.

More samples than pixels need a display rule

A line chart with hundreds of thousands of readings across a 900-pixel plot cannot show each reading distinctly. Sending every point still costs transfer, parsing, memory, layout and interaction time. A random sample or every-50th-point stride can erase a brief but operationally important spike. Decide whether the reader is inspecting shape, extrema, exact intervals or anomalies. The chart task determines the reduction method. The full-resolution data remains the source; the plotted series is a deliberately derived view.

Preserve a bounded envelope

For each time bucket, retain its first, last, minimum and maximum observations, ordered by timestamp and deduplicated by identity. This keeps endpoints connected and exposes local peaks and troughs that a mean would smooth away. It is not lossless: the order of several internal turns and narrow oscillations may still be compressed. Show the bucket width or resolution when it affects interpretation, and fetch raw samples on zoom or request. If missing intervals exist, split segments before reducing; joining across a gap creates a fictional line. Gap policy applies before level of detail.

Build levels against stable data versions

Precomputed hourly, daily or pixel-width buckets must use a fixed time origin and a named aggregation function. If a late event revises an old bucket, invalidate that level together with raw data. Cache keys need range, resolution, filters, unit and source generation. A multi-resolution chart can request a coarser level during pan, then replace it with fine points after the interaction settles; label provisional rendering when it might change a decision. Serving freshness constrains what a pre-aggregated chart can claim.

Keep exactness available

Tooltips on reduced marks should describe the bucket, extrema and sample count. Calling a retained minimum a point-in-time average is wrong. A downloadable CSV should offer the filtered raw interval or clearly name the reduced level. If a user clicks a peak to investigate a machine stoppage, resolve it to source IDs rather than an arbitrary nearby display point. The export manifest should state whether the series is raw or reduced.

Measure end-to-end cost

Track transfer bytes, parse time, memory, first paint, pan latency and number of marks actually drawn. A server-side envelope can reduce browser work but adds query and cache-maintenance cost. A canvas renderer can draw many marks faster than DOM-based SVG, yet it needs deliberate keyboard and text alternatives. Test a single-sample range, identical timestamps, gaps and a narrow spike at each bucket boundary. The acceptance check is not only a speedup: the operational alert must remain visible at the default zoom.

Worked contract

def extrema_envelope(samples: list[tuple[int, float]],
                     bucket_size: int) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    if bucket_size < 1 or any(samples[index][0] >= samples[index + 1][0]
                               for index in range(len(samples) - 1)):
        raise ValueError("bucket size or time order is invalid")
    reduced = []
    for start in range(0, len(samples), bucket_size):
        bucket = samples[start:start + bucket_size]
        selected = {bucket[0], bucket[-1],
                    min(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1]),
                    max(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1])}
        reduced.extend(sorted(selected, key=lambda point: point[0]))
    return reduced

readings = [(47, 4.0), (48, 4.1), (49, 81.0), (50, 4.2),
            (51, 4.0), (52, 3.9)]
visible = extrema_envelope(readings, 4)
assert (49, 81.0) in visible and visible[0] == readings[0]
assert len(visible) <= 4 * ((len(readings) + 3) // 4)

Performance and operating cost

For N sorted samples and bucket size B, the demonstration runs in O(N + (N/B) log 4) time and emits at most four observations per bucket, O(N/B) output space. Python slices hold up to O(B) temporary items. It assumes strictly increasing timestamps and one continuous segment; production data with same-time events needs an explicit tie policy, and gaps need separate segments. Maintaining a pyramid of levels increases storage but can make viewport requests proportional to visible resolution rather than total history.

Common Mistakes

  • Taking every nth reading and deleting a short-lived alarm spike.
  • Reducing across a missing-data gap and drawing a continuous line.
  • Calling a retained minimum or maximum a bucket average.
  • Caching a reduced level without the filter and source-version keys.

Validation drill

Reduce a 47,000-point sensor series to a 900-pixel view. Insert 19 one-point spikes at varied bucket positions and verify every spike survives the chosen display reduction; compare load and pan times with the raw series.

title: Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together
summary: Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.
body:
Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.

An image is not the full evidence

A PNG captures pixels; it does not preserve the records, filter predicates, missingness states or exact values behind them. SVG retains scalable geometry, but it can still omit the underlying analytical contract. For a decision-grade chart, export an image, a machine-readable table of plotted values and a manifest describing the query and rendering choices. The package should answer which source snapshot, cohort, units, time zone, grouping rule, axis domain, palette and code version produced the picture. Dashboard provenance supplies these ingredients; export binds them to an artifact.

Version the plotted data product

A chart may use raw events, daily aggregates or a reduced display level. The export must name that level. Include a dataset snapshot or immutable revision, plus the report's as-of time when corrections are possible. A hash of canonical manifest bytes detects accidental changes to the manifest; it does not authenticate a source by itself. If integrity across systems matters, sign the package through a trusted release path. Never include private identifiers or unmasked rows merely because a chart view was authorized. Data classification still governs exports.

Keep visible and downloadable values aligned

The CSV or JSON table must use the same filters, denominator, sort, unit and missing-value policy as the displayed chart. If the chart shows rounded percentages, include underlying counts and unrounded rates in the data export while documenting the display rounding. A tooltip, table and image title should agree on the period and finalization status. Linked filters can change the cohort moments before a user clicks export; capture one state and one data version atomically for the whole package.

Make the visual portable and accessible

An SVG is useful for vector editing and high-resolution print, but font substitution and external styles can change its appearance. A PNG is more predictable but loses scale and selectable text. Include an accessible text summary and data table in either case. Document the output size, color profile where relevant, and the scale tick labels. Text alternatives should describe the main pattern, notable exceptions and uncertainty rather than repeat a generic chart title. For a public download, test that no hidden private series remain in SVG markup or embedded metadata.

Recreate before release

Re-run the export from its manifest in a clean environment. Compare plotted counts, axis limits, filters, title, source generation and checksum, allowing only declared rendering differences such as font rasterization. A changed query definition should make an old package non-reproducible by design; report that conflict instead of silently rendering with today's code. Keep an editorial preview for review, then publish an immutable artifact reference when the chart is used in a report or audit. Reduced series need the level and bucket rule in the manifest.

Worked contract

import hashlib
import json

def chart_manifest(query_id: str, dataset_version: str,
                   filters: dict[str, list[str]],
                   axis_domain: tuple[float, float],
                   plotted_rows: int) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    if not query_id or not dataset_version or plotted_rows < 0:
        raise ValueError("missing chart identity")
    if axis_domain[0] >= axis_domain[1]:
        raise ValueError("invalid axis domain")
    manifest = {
        "query_id": query_id,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "filters": {key: sorted(set(values))
                    for key, values in sorted(filters.items())},
        "y_axis_domain": list(axis_domain),
        "plotted_rows": plotted_rows,
        "unit": "minutes",
        "render_contract": "depot-delay-v3",
    }
    payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                         ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
    return manifest, hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

first = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                       {"region": ["north", "north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
second = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                        {"region": ["north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
assert first == second and len(first[1]) == 64

Performance and operating cost

For F total filter values and M serialized manifest bytes, sorting normalized filters costs O(F log F) in the worst case; JSON encoding and SHA-256 hashing take O(M) time and O(M) temporary memory. Exporting an image or plotted data can cost much more and depends on the renderer and row count. This hash identifies equal manifest bytes, not equal pixels or trustworthy provenance. Add a data-file checksum and a signed release record when the export package crosses a trust boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Publishing only a screenshot when reviewers need the plotted data and cohort definition.
  • Exporting a CSV from a stale filter state while the chart shows a newer selection.
  • Assuming a manifest hash proves who created the data.
  • Embedding hidden private rows in an otherwise public SVG or HTML export.

Validation drill

Export one filtered depot-delay chart as SVG and CSV with a manifest. Change only the filter and verify the manifest digest changes, then rebuild the original chart from its saved version and compare counts and axis bounds.

title: Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
summary: Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.
body:
Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.

Begin with observations

A box summarizes a group's quartiles and median; a violin adds an estimated density shape. Neither replaces the sample size. A smooth violin made from seven delivery times can look as confident as one made from seven thousand. Put each group's count beside its label and show individual points for small groups. Distribution and outlier displays explain what the summary hides. First check whether groups cover the same window, unit and eligibility rule. Otherwise the apparent difference may be a cohort change.

Declare the quartile rule

Software packages can interpolate quartiles differently, and whiskers may mean the extrema or a multiple of the interquartile range. State the rule in the chart caption or export record. A point beyond a whisker is not automatically bad data; it is flagged under that rule. If the decision needs the fraction exceeding a service threshold, calculate that fraction directly rather than asking a box to imply it. An empirical CDF answers threshold questions without a smoothing choice.

Treat bandwidth as a parameter

A violin's width depends on a density estimate and its bandwidth. A wide bandwidth can merge two real modes; a narrow one can turn routine noise into several peaks. Compare more than one defensible bandwidth, retain a rug or points, and do not imply that a thin tail continues beyond a physical limit. The mirrored shape is a drawing convention, not a second population. Normalize violin widths by count only if width should carry count. Otherwise make widths equal and show counts separately. Grain and denominator still matter.

Keep groups comparable

Use the same quantitative axis, bandwidth rule and density normalization across groups. Truncating each group to its own range can make spreads seem alike. For latency data, inspect zeros, censored values and caps before estimating density. If the data include repeated readings from the same device, an independent violin discards pairing. A paired view retains it. Supply a text table with each count, median, quartiles and threshold exceedance for readers who cannot use the shape.

Worked contract

def quartile_summary(readings: list[float]) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    from math import isfinite
    if not readings or any(not isfinite(value) for value in readings):
        raise ValueError("readings must be finite and nonempty")
    ordered = sorted(readings)
    def midpoint(values: list[float]) -> float:
        middle = len(values) // 2
        return (values[middle] if len(values) % 2 else
                (values[middle - 1] + values[middle]) / 2)
    middle = len(ordered) // 2
    lower = ordered[:middle]
    upper = ordered[middle + len(ordered) % 2:]
    return {"count": len(ordered), "median": midpoint(ordered),
            "q1": midpoint(lower) if lower else ordered[0],
            "q3": midpoint(upper) if upper else ordered[0]}

depot_latency = quartile_summary([47, 51, 59, 68, 81, 83, 96])
assert depot_latency == {"count": 7, "median": 68, "q1": 51, "q3": 83}

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N observations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for the ordered copy. A chart with G groups repeats this per group; density estimation adds work set by the estimator and evaluation grid. The code declares a median-of-halves quartile convention and handles a one-item group. It does not draw a violin or claim that seven points support a smooth density. Store the exact convention with the exported summary.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a smooth violin for a tiny group without points.
  • Comparing boxes whose whiskers use different rules.
  • Treating a flagged point as an invalid measurement.
  • Changing density bandwidth between groups and reading widths as a real difference.

Validation drill

Compare response times for three depots with 7, 47 and 810 records. Print each count, median and quartile rule; draw points for the smallest group, then inspect whether two bandwidth choices alter the visual claim.
